Wells affect each other · Simulation: 450 test wells

When one well pumps, its neighbours feel it.

Groundwater is shared. Pumping one borewell can lower the water in others, sometimes kilometres away. Knowing these links would show where pumping hurts the whole area most. We built a model to learn them and tested it on a simulated city where the true links are known.

In the drawing: pumping at A reaches C through the crack. B is closer but barely affected.

Why distance isn't enough

Under Bengaluru, groundwater sits in cracks in hard rock. Two wells on the same crack can affect each other even far apart, while close neighbours may not.

So the model combines two inputs. A geology map of likely cracks tells it who may be connected. The monitoring data tells it how strongly.

Pressure points: whose pumping hurts the whole area most?

Each dot is a simulated well. The darker it is, the more the whole area's water sinks when that well pumps more. Lines are mapped cracks, the geology map the model was given.

What the model got right

Tested on a second simulated city that played no part in building the model.

If 30 wells cut pumping by a quarter, which 30 should it be?

—

The figure is the rise in water level summed over all wells, per 1,000 m³ of pumping cut, over 30 days of simulation.

What this shows
    What it cannot do yet
    • Pin down the exact link between two specific wells, or how many days it takes. Daily data is too coarse; that needs a short pumping test logged minute by minute.
    • Run on the real wells: we do not yet have their locations.
    • This is a simulation. Real crack networks are messier.

    What it would take to do this for real →

    Borewell Forecast is a proof of concept for forecasting groundwater levels in Bengaluru borewells. Results are labelled by where the data came from: real pump data (15 days, July 2026), synthetic test system (450 simulated wells with a known answer) or digital twin (a physics-based simulation of the 579 wells over a year). Nothing here is yet a validated field forecast.
